note: Dante's Italian adds here "that my comedy does not care to sing". It is one of only two places where he calls his poem a comedy, and it comes just after Virgil has called the Aeneid his tragedy. The translation says "my story".

context: This is the fifth of its ten ditches. Dante spends more than two cantos here, longer than in any other ditch so far.

note: The great state shipyard of Venice, founded in the twelfth century and among the largest workshops in medieval Europe. In winter, when ships could not sail, the fleet was repaired there. The busy, even cheerful picture of men at work makes the dark ditch that follows darker.
Tar, boiled and pressed into the seams of a hull to make it watertight.

The ditch of the barrators, or grafters: officials who sold public offices, favors and justice for bribes. It is the civil crime that matches simony in the Church. They dealt in secret and had sticky fingers, so they are kept under a black surface that clings to them and hides them.
The sinners are all below the surface. Graft is done out of sight.

Graft was the charge on which Florence condemned Dante himself in 1302 and sent him into exile. He always denied it. Readers have long linked that to the fear and the danger he shows in this ditch, more than anywhere else in Hell.
The elders were the chief magistrates of Lucca, a council of ten. The demon doesn't name this one. An early commentator identifies him as Martino Bottaio, a Lucchese official who died in 1300.

context: Zita was a serving woman of Lucca who died in the 1270s. The people of the city already honored her as a saint, long before the Church made it official.

note: Sarcasm. Bonturo Dati, a leader of the popular party in Lucca in the early 1300s, was known as the worst grafter of them all. He was still alive when Dante wrote.

quote: they turn No to Yes for cash
note: In the Italian the demon uses the Latin word "ita", yes, the language of official documents. For money, a refusal on paper becomes a permission.
He comes up doubled over, with his back in the air, like a man bowing in prayer. That is the cue for the demons' joke about the Holy Face.

The Volto Santo, an ancient wooden crucifix in the cathedral of Lucca, said to have been carved by Nicodemus, who helped bury Christ. The people of Lucca prayed to it in trouble, and it was famous across Europe.
The river that runs past Lucca, where its people swam in summer.

quote: grab what you can in secret
note: The demons taunt him with his own sin: he took bribes under cover, so let him try stealing under the pitch.
The comparisons in these two cantos come from kitchens, kennels and farmyards. The style drops with the subject: this is the comic, coarse episode of the Inferno, sometimes called the devils' farce.

quote: I've been in such a fight before
note: Virgil has been down through Hell once already, sent by a witch soon after his death (Inferno 9). He has also faced the devils at the gate of Dis, where they shut him out and only an angel got him through (Inferno 8–9). His confidence here will prove misplaced.
The bank on the far side of the fifth ditch, which divides it from the sixth.
The formula that has opened every door in Hell since Charon and Minos (Inferno 3 and 5). It works again, but only on the surface: Malacoda obeys and then lies.

A castle of Pisa on the river Arno. In August 1289 it surrendered to the army of Florence and Lucca, and its garrison marched out between the ranks of their enemies under a promise of safety. Dante says he saw it, the best evidence that he served in that campaign, at twenty-four.
The name suggests someone who ruffles or tousles: a brawler.
The bridge over the sixth ditch, the next span of the ridge the poets have been following. This part is true: it has fallen.
A lie, and the trap of the whole episode. Every bridge over the sixth ditch is broken. Virgil believes him, and learns the truth only in Inferno 23.

quote: Yesterday, five hours later than now
note: The poem's clearest statement of its own date. The road broke in the earthquake at Christ's death (Matthew 27:51), which Dante placed at noon on Good Friday in the thirty-fourth year of Christ's life. Add 1,266 years and it is 1300. "Yesterday" was Good Friday, and it is now seven in the morning of Holy Saturday.
The same earthquake caused the landslide Dante climbed down in Inferno 12. A devil dates everything in his world from the day Christ died and broke into Hell.
Coming up out of the pitch for relief. The patrol's job is to hook any sinner who shows himself.

The devils' names are Dante's inventions, half comic and half threatening. Alichino may be related to Harlequin, who began as a demon in French folklore. Calcabrina is something like "Frost-trampler".
"Nasty dog". Several of the names sound like twisted versions of real family names of Florence and Lucca, and some scholars think Dante was mocking officials of his day.
"Curly-beard", the sergeant of the patrol. He leads ten devils, a mock version of a military squad.
Libicocco may combine the names of two winds, the libeccio and the sirocco. Draghignazzo suggests a big, ugly dragon.
Ciriatto is "Hog", from a word for a pig. Graffiacane is "Dog-scratcher".
Farfarello was a name for a goblin or imp in Italian folklore. Rubicante is "Red-face".

quote: Keep these two safe until the next ridge
note: Since no such ridge exists, the safe conduct is worth nothing, and the devils know it. That is what their grins and signals mean.
Dante, who is afraid, reads the devils correctly. Virgil, who stands for reason, is taken in. Fraud is the one thing reason alone is slow to see through.

quote: he made a trumpet of his ass
note: A parody of an army moving off at a trumpet call, and the most famous vulgar line in the poem. Dante held that a comedy could use every level of language, down to the lowest. The next canto opens by dwelling on this signal.
